lesson_title: The CPU and Von Neumann Architecture
content_html:
What Is the CPU?

The CPU is the brain of any computer system. It carries out the instructions that make up every program you run — from loading a webpage to running a game. Without the CPU, no processing can happen. Every calculation, decision and data movement passes through this single chip.

The design that almost every modern CPU is built on was described by mathematician John von Neumann in 1945. Von Neumann architecture states that a program’s instructions and its data should be stored in the same memory, and that the CPU should fetch each instruction in sequence, decode it, and then execute it. This idea — so straightforward it seems obvious now — was revolutionary at the time and remains the foundation of almost every computer built today.

Key Fact

A CPU contains two main sub-units: the Control Unit (CU), which manages the fetch-decode-execute cycle, and the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), which performs calculations and logical comparisons.

The Control Unit

The Control Unit (CU) acts as the conductor of the CPU. It does not process data itself — instead it sends control signals that tell every other component what to do and when to do it. The CU reads the current instruction, works out what operation is needed, and then triggers the correct sequence of actions across the CPU, memory and input/output devices.

Think of the CU as a traffic controller at a busy junction: it does not drive any of the vehicles, but without it the whole system would grind to a halt. Every time your computer opens a file or responds to a keystroke, the CU is orchestrating the response.

The Arithmetic Logic Unit

The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is the calculator inside the CPU. It handles two types of operation. Arithmetic operations include addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — used whenever a program works with numbers. Logical operations include AND, OR, NOT and comparisons (is A greater than B? are two values equal?) — used every time a program makes a decision.

When you sort a list of names alphabetically, the ALU is comparing characters thousands of times per second. When a game calculates a bullet’s trajectory, the ALU is doing the maths. The ALU receives its inputs from registers (small, fast storage locations inside the CPU), performs the operation, and places the result back into a register.

Registers

Registers are tiny storage locations built directly into the CPU chip. Because they sit so close to the processing circuits, they are the fastest storage in any computer system — far faster than even cache or RAM. The specification names five key registers you must know:

  • Program Counter (PC) — holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched. It increments automatically after each fetch so that instructions are processed in order (unless a jump instruction changes it).
  • Memory Address Register (MAR) — holds the address in memory that the CPU is about to read from or write to.
  • Memory Data Register (MDR) — holds the data that has just been read from memory, or the data that is about to be written to memory. It acts as a buffer between the CPU and RAM.
  • Current Instruction Register (CIR) — holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed. While the CIR is busy, the PC can already move on to the address of the next instruction.
  • Accumulator (ACC) — the register where the ALU stores the results of arithmetic and logical operations. When two numbers are added, the answer lands in the ACC.
Key Fact

The five named registers are: PC (address of the next instruction), MAR (address being accessed in memory), MDR (data travelling to/from memory), CIR (the current instruction being executed) and ACC (the result of ALU calculations).

Cache Memory

Cache memory sits between the CPU and main memory (RAM). Accessing RAM takes far longer than accessing the CPU’s own circuits — if the CPU had to fetch every instruction directly from RAM, it would spend most of its time waiting. Cache solves this problem by storing copies of recently used or frequently needed instructions close to the processor.

Cache is organised into levels. L1 cache is the smallest and fastest (typically 32–64 KB per core), built directly into the processor core. L2 cache is larger (256 KB–1 MB) and slightly slower. L3 cache is shared between cores and can reach 8–32 MB on modern chips. When the CPU needs data, it checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only falls back to RAM if all levels fail to supply it.

In Von Neumann architecture, both the program being executed and the data it operates on are stored together in RAM. This is significant: it means a program can treat other programs as data and modify itself — the basis of all modern software.

RAM is volatile, meaning it loses all its contents the moment power is removed. This is why you must save a document before switching off your computer — anything in RAM that has not been written to a storage device is lost. The CPU reads instructions from RAM into the MDR, then passes them to the CIR for decoding. It also reads data values from RAM for the ALU to process, and writes results back to RAM when needed.

The amount of RAM a computer has directly affects how many programs it can run at once. If RAM fills up, the operating system must resort to virtual memory — using part of the secondary storage device as an overflow area. Because secondary storage is far slower than RAM, this causes a significant performance drop.

Misconception 1: The CU does calculations. It does not. The CU only controls and coordinates — all calculations go to the ALU. A common exam error is stating that the CU “adds numbers together” or “processes data”.

Misconception 2: Cache is the same as RAM. Cache is much smaller, much faster, and located on or very close to the CPU die. RAM is separate from the CPU and connects via the memory bus. They serve different purposes: cache reduces the time the CPU spends waiting; RAM stores all running programs and their data.

Misconception 3: The MAR stores the data, and the MDR stores the address. It’s the other way round. MAR = address, MDR = data. A helpful reminder: Address goes in the Address register (MAR); Data goes in the Data register (MDR).

The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

Every program your computer runs — from a simple calculator to a complex video game — is ultimately a list of instructions stored in memory. The Fetch-Decode-Execute (FDE) cycle is the process a CPU uses to work through those instructions, one at a time, billions of times per second. Understanding the cycle also means understanding exactly which register does what during each stage.

Stage 1 — Fetch

The cycle begins with the CPU needing to retrieve the next instruction from main memory (RAM). Here is the sequence of register operations during the fetch stage:

  1. The Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. This address is copied into the Memory Address Register (MAR).
  2. The PC is immediately incremented so it points to the address of the instruction after that — ready for the following cycle.
  3. The CPU sends the address in the MAR along the address bus to RAM. RAM returns the instruction at that address along the data bus into the Memory Data Register (MDR).
  4. The instruction is copied from the MDR into the Current Instruction Register (CIR), where it waits to be decoded.
Key Fact

During the Fetch stage: PC holds the instruction’s address → address copied to MAR → PC increments → instruction retrieved from RAM into MDR → instruction copied to CIR.

Stage 2 — Decode

With the instruction safely in the CIR, the Decode stage begins. The Control Unit (CU) reads the instruction from the CIR and splits it into two parts: the opcode, which specifies the operation to perform (e.g. ADD, LOAD, STORE, JUMP), and the operand, which specifies the data or memory address involved.

For example, an instruction might say “ADD the value at memory address 200 to the Accumulator.” The opcode is ADD, and the operand is the address 200. The CU then prepares the appropriate circuits and control signals for the execute stage.

Stage 3 — Execute

The CU carries out the decoded instruction by sending control signals to the correct components. The exact actions depend on the instruction type:

  • Arithmetic or logic instruction (e.g. ADD, AND): the operand is passed to the ALU, which performs the operation and places the result in the Accumulator (ACC).
  • Load instruction: the operand’s address is placed in the MAR, the data is fetched from RAM into the MDR, and then copied into the ACC.
  • Store instruction: the value in the ACC is placed in the MDR, the target address goes into the MAR, and the data is written from the MDR to RAM.
  • Jump instruction: the operand (a memory address) overwrites the PC, so the next fetch stage begins at a different location in the program. This is how loops and branches work.

Once execution is complete, the cycle immediately repeats: the PC already holds the address of the next instruction, so the fetch stage begins again without any pause.

Key Fact

Three factors affect CPU performance: clock speed (more cycles per second means more instructions executed per second), number of cores (more cores allow more instruction streams to be processed simultaneously), and cache size (more cache means fewer slow RAM accesses).

CPU Performance Factor 1 — Clock Speed

Clock speed is how many FDE cycles the CPU completes every second. It is measured in hertz (Hz), but modern processors run at several gigahertz (GHz) — billions of cycles per second. A 3.5 GHz processor completes 3,500,000,000 cycles every second.

Increasing the clock speed means each instruction completes faster, so programs run more quickly. However, a higher clock speed generates more heat and uses more power. This is why processors come with cooling systems and why laptops throttle (reduce) their clock speed when they overheat.

CPU Performance Factor 2 — Number of Cores

A core is a complete processing unit with its own CU, ALU and registers. A single-core CPU can only execute one instruction stream at a time. A multi-core CPU (dual-core, quad-core, octa-core) can run multiple instruction streams in parallel.

If you have a quad-core processor, your computer can run four independent streams of instructions simultaneously — one per core. This is why modern computers run many applications at once without slowing to a crawl. However, software must be written to take advantage of multiple cores; a single-threaded program only ever uses one core, no matter how many are available.

CPU Performance Factor 3 — Cache Size

Cache is the fastest memory available to the CPU, but it is very expensive to manufacture. A larger cache means the CPU can hold more instructions and data close at hand, reducing the number of times it must wait for a RAM access. When the CPU looks for data and finds it in cache (a ‘cache hit’), it can proceed immediately. When it does not find it (a ‘cache miss’), it must stall and wait for RAM — which can take 100 or more times longer than a cache access.

Suppose the PC holds the value 100, meaning the next instruction is stored at memory address 100. Trace through the cycle:

  1. Fetch: Address 100 is copied from PC to MAR. PC increments to 101. The instruction at address 100 is fetched from RAM via the data bus into the MDR. The instruction is copied from MDR to CIR.
  2. Decode: The CU reads the instruction in the CIR. Suppose the opcode is ADD and the operand is 50 (meaning “add the value at address 50 to the ACC”). The CU prepares the ALU and sets up address 50 for a memory read.
  3. Execute: Address 50 is placed in the MAR. The value at address 50 is fetched into the MDR. The ALU adds this value to the current contents of the ACC. The result is placed back in the ACC. The cycle immediately repeats from PC = 101.

This step-by-step register trace is exactly what exam questions ask you to produce in a ‘trace the FDE cycle’ question. Practice following the data through each register in order.

Doubling the number of cores does not double the speed of every program. Amdahl’s Law describes this: if 50% of a program must run sequentially (one instruction after another, with no parallelism), the maximum possible speedup from adding more cores is 2× — no matter how many cores you add.

Tasks that can be split into independent parallel chunks (e.g. rendering different sections of a 3D scene, running separate browser tabs) benefit greatly from more cores. Tasks that have strict dependencies between steps (e.g. calculating the next step in a physics simulation) benefit much less. This is why examiners expect you to qualify your answer when explaining cores as a performance factor: “more cores improve performance provided the software is written to use multiple threads”.

Why Computers Need Different Types of Storage

No single storage technology can do everything well. The storage inside a computer is organised into a hierarchy: the fastest storage sits closest to the CPU (registers, then cache), but it is tiny and expensive. Cheaper, larger storage sits further away but takes longer to access. Understanding where each type fits — and why — is essential for your exam.

Storage falls into two broad categories. Primary storage is directly accessible by the CPU: it includes RAM, ROM, cache and flash memory. Secondary storage is not directly accessible by the CPU; files must be loaded into primary storage before the CPU can work with them.

RAM — Random Access Memory

RAM is the computer’s main working memory. Everything the CPU is actively using — the operating system, open applications, files being edited — is held in RAM. RAM is volatile: it loses all its contents when power is removed. It is also read/write: the CPU can both read from it and write to it during normal operation.

The more RAM a computer has, the more programs it can keep open simultaneously without slowing down. A typical modern desktop might have 8 GB to 32 GB of RAM. RAM connects to the CPU via the memory bus; access time is around 50–100 nanoseconds, much slower than cache but far faster than any secondary storage device.

ROM — Read-Only Memory

ROM is non-volatile — it keeps its contents when the power is off. As its name suggests, it is read-only under normal operation: the CPU can read from it but cannot change its contents during normal use. ROM holds firmware such as the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System), which runs first when a computer starts, checking hardware and loading the operating system from secondary storage.

Because ROM retains data without power, it is ideal for storing start-up instructions. Without ROM, a computer would not know how to begin loading the operating system after being switched on.

Flash Memory and Virtual Memory

Flash memory is a form of non-volatile storage that can be both read from and written to without requiring power to retain its data. USB flash drives, SD cards, smartphones and solid-state drives all use flash memory. Because it has no moving parts, it is more durable than magnetic hard drives and faster to access.

Virtual memory is not a physical component but a technique. When RAM fills up, the operating system moves the least-recently-used sections of RAM to a reserved area on the secondary storage device (a ‘page file’ or ‘swap space’). This frees up RAM for the task currently in use. The downside is significant: secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so heavy use of virtual memory causes the system to slow dramatically — a problem called thrashing.

Key Fact

Volatile (loses data without power): RAM, cache. Non-volatile (retains data without power): ROM, flash memory, all secondary storage devices. Virtual memory uses secondary storage, so it is non-volatile, but using it is slow.

Secondary Storage — The Four Types

Secondary storage provides permanent, high-capacity storage for files, programs and data. There are four types you must be able to compare on five criteria: capacity, durability, portability, speed and cost.

Magnetic Storage (HDD)

Magnetic hard disk drives (HDDs) store data as tiny magnetised regions on spinning metal platters. A moving read/write head swings over the platter surface to read or write data. HDDs offer very high capacity (up to several TB for consumer drives) at a relatively low cost per gigabyte. However, the mechanical moving parts make them slower than solid-state alternatives and more vulnerable to physical shock.

Solid-State Storage (SSD)

Solid-state drives (SSDs) use the same flash memory technology as USB drives, but in a larger, faster form. Because there are no moving parts, SSDs access data much faster than HDDs (access times measured in microseconds rather than milliseconds), are silent, run cooler, and withstand knocks and drops far better. The trade-off is cost: SSDs cost significantly more per gigabyte than HDDs, though the gap has narrowed in recent years.

Optical Storage

Optical storage uses a laser to read (and sometimes write) data encoded on a disc surface. CDs hold around 700 MB, DVDs 4.7 GB (or 8.5 GB dual-layer) and Blu-ray discs up to 50 GB. Optical media is highly portable and cheap per disc, but access speed is slow compared to SSDs and HDDs, and discs can be scratched, making them less durable for frequent daily use.

Cloud Storage

Cloud storage stores files on remote servers accessed via the internet, such as Google Drive, OneDrive or iCloud. From the user’s perspective, files are available on any internet-connected device anywhere in the world. Capacity is theoretically unlimited (you simply pay for more storage). However, access speed depends on the internet connection, and there are concerns about security (files held by a third party) and privacy (who can access the data). If the internet connection fails, files may be temporarily inaccessible.

Key Fact

Comparison summary: SSDs are faster and more durable than HDDs but more expensive per GB. HDDs offer higher capacity per pound. Optical media is cheap and portable but slow and scratchable. Cloud storage is accessible anywhere but needs internet and raises security concerns.

This exam uses base-2 prefixes for storage calculations. This is critical because answers using base-10 are marked as incorrect on calculation questions:

  • 1 KB (kilobyte) = \(2^{10}\) = 1,024 bytes
  • 1 MB (megabyte) = \(2^{20}\) = 1,048,576 bytes
  • 1 GB (gigabyte) = \(2^{30}\) = 1,073,741,824 bytes

For image storage calculations: multiply width (pixels) × height (pixels) × bit depth (bits per pixel). This gives the total in bits. Divide by 8 to get bytes, then divide by 1,024 repeatedly for KB, MB, GB. Forgetting to divide by 8 at the first step is the most common error.

Beyond the CPU: Additional Hardware

The CPU is the heart of any computer, but it does not work alone. Several additional hardware components are essential to how a modern computer operates. This lesson covers three named components from the specification: the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit), the sound card, and the motherboard. Understanding what each one does — and how they connect to the rest of the system — is tested directly in the theory paper.

The GPU — Graphics Processing Unit

A GPU is a specialised processor built to handle graphics. Displaying a single frame on a modern screen can require millions of calculations — working out the colour, brightness and position of each pixel. The CPU could theoretically do this, but it would be extremely slow because CPUs have relatively few, powerful cores optimised for serial tasks.

A GPU contains thousands of smaller, simpler cores that work in parallel. This makes GPUs far better than CPUs at performing the same simple calculation (such as “what colour is this pixel?”) on many pieces of data simultaneously. As a result, a GPU can render complex 3D scenes, play 4K video and run visual effects smoothly in real time.

GPUs also have applications beyond graphics. Because of their parallel architecture, they are now used for machine learning, scientific simulation, cryptocurrency mining and video encoding — any workload that involves doing the same calculation on thousands of data points at once.

Integrated vs Dedicated GPUs

There are two configurations you must know for your exam:

An integrated GPU is built directly onto the same chip (or die) as the CPU. It shares the computer’s main RAM as its video memory. Integrated GPUs consume less power, generate less heat and keep costs down, making them ideal for laptops, tablets and everyday computing tasks like web browsing, word processing and streaming video. However, because they share RAM, they perform less well when running graphically demanding applications.

A dedicated GPU (also called a discrete GPU) is a separate expansion card that plugs into the motherboard. It has its own dedicated video memory (VRAM) — separate from the system’s RAM — which gives it much higher bandwidth for graphics data. Dedicated GPUs are used in gaming computers, video editing workstations and servers running artificial intelligence. They are significantly more powerful than integrated GPUs but also more expensive, larger and more power-hungry.

Key Fact

An integrated GPU is built into the CPU chip and shares main RAM. A dedicated GPU is a separate card with its own VRAM. Integrated GPUs suit everyday use; dedicated GPUs are needed for gaming, video editing and machine learning.

The Sound Card

A sound card handles all audio input and output for a computer. It performs two conversions:

  • Digital to Analogue Conversion (DAC): When you play music or a game, the audio is stored as digital data (binary numbers). The sound card converts this to an analogue electrical signal that a speaker can turn into sound waves.
  • Analogue to Digital Conversion (ADC): When you speak into a microphone or record an instrument, the sound card converts the analogue electrical signal from the microphone into digital data that the computer can process and store.

Like the GPU, sound cards come in two forms. Most modern computers have an integrated sound card built into the motherboard, which is sufficient for everyday use (music, video calls, gaming). Dedicated (discrete) sound cards are used by musicians, audio engineers and broadcasters who need higher quality audio, more inputs/outputs, or lower latency than the integrated solution provides.

Key Fact

A sound card performs Digital-to-Analogue Conversion (DAC) for audio playback (turning binary data into sound waves via a speaker) and Analogue-to-Digital Conversion (ADC) for audio input (turning a microphone’s electrical signal into digital data the CPU can process).

The Motherboard

The motherboard is the central circuit board that everything else connects to. It does not process data itself; instead, it provides the physical connections and communication pathways that allow every component to work together as a system.

The key features of a motherboard include:

  • CPU socket: the slot that holds the CPU. The socket type must match the CPU model (e.g. Intel LGA and AMD AM5 sockets are not interchangeable).
  • RAM slots: connectors for main memory modules. A typical motherboard has 2–8 RAM slots.
  • Expansion slots: long connectors (usually PCIe — Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) into which dedicated GPUs, sound cards, network cards and other expansion cards plug.
  • Storage connectors: SATA and M.2 connectors for HDDs, SSDs and optical drives.
  • Buses: the data pathways printed directly onto the motherboard. The data bus carries data between components; the address bus carries memory addresses; the control bus carries control signals from the CPU. Bus width (measured in bits) and bus speed (measured in MHz or GHz) both affect system performance.
  • ROM chip (BIOS/UEFI): the motherboard holds the system’s firmware, which runs when the computer starts up before the operating system loads.
  • External ports: USB, HDMI, audio jacks and network sockets are mounted directly on the motherboard, connecting peripherals to the system.

A bus is a set of electrical pathways (wires or printed traces) that carries signals between components. The motherboard contains three buses connecting the CPU to everything else:

  • Data bus — carries the actual data being transferred (e.g. the contents of the MDR moving to RAM). It is bidirectional: data can travel either way.
  • Address bus — carries memory addresses (e.g. the contents of the MAR). It is unidirectional: the CPU sends addresses, but addresses do not flow back.
  • Control bus — carries control signals from the CU (e.g. “read” or “write” signals that tell RAM whether to accept or send data). Also bidirectional (some signals go from CPU to memory; interrupt signals go from devices to CPU).

A wider data bus (more parallel wires) means more bits can be transferred in one go. A 64-bit data bus can transfer 8 bytes per clock cycle, whereas a 32-bit bus transfers only 4 bytes. Bus speed (measured in MHz) multiplied by bus width determines bandwidth — the maximum data transfer rate.

Training a machine learning model requires applying the same mathematical operation to millions of numbers simultaneously — exactly the type of work GPUs were designed for. A high-end GPU can contain over 10,000 cores, each handling a small piece of the calculation in parallel. Modern AI language models and image generators are trained on clusters of hundreds of GPUs working together.

This “general-purpose GPU computing” (sometimes called GPGPU) means that when you hear about a company building a supercomputer for AI research, the majority of its processing power comes from GPUs rather than traditional CPUs. In your exam, this context may appear in ‘Discuss Impacts’ questions about AI or high-performance computing.

What Is an Embedded System?

When most people think of a computer, they picture a laptop or a desktop machine with a keyboard, screen and operating system. But the vast majority of computers in the world are not general-purpose machines — they are embedded systems: computers hidden inside everyday objects, each dedicated to performing one specific job.

Your washing machine, microwave, car’s anti-lock braking system, traffic lights, heart rate monitor, and the thermostat on your central heating all contain embedded systems. In fact, there are estimated to be roughly 30 billion embedded processors in use worldwide — compared to fewer than 2 billion general-purpose computers. Embedded systems massively outnumber conventional computers.

Key Characteristics of Embedded Systems

Embedded systems share a set of defining characteristics that distinguish them from general-purpose computers. Understanding these is essential for exam questions that ask you to “describe the characteristics of” or “explain why a device is described as an embedded system.”

1. Dedicated function. An embedded system is designed to perform one specific task. A washing machine controller manages wash cycles; it cannot be used to browse the internet or run a spreadsheet. This is the opposite of a general-purpose computer, which can run many different programs.

2. Real-time operation. Most embedded systems must respond to events within a guaranteed time period. A car’s anti-lock braking system (ABS) must detect wheel lock-up and release the brakes within milliseconds — any longer and the response is too late to be useful. This requirement for predictable, guaranteed timing is called real-time operation.

3. Low power consumption. Many embedded systems run on batteries (fitness bands, pacemakers, remote controls) or must run continuously for years without attention (smart meters, industrial sensors). They are designed to use as little power as possible.

4. Low cost. Because embedded systems are mass-produced in billions of units (every microwave sold contains one), cost is critical. Embedded processors are simplified, cheap microcontrollers rather than the powerful, expensive chips found in PCs.

5. Reliability. An embedded system inside a pacemaker or an aircraft’s flight management system must work correctly every time, without crashing. Unlike a PC that can be rebooted when it freezes, many embedded systems run safety-critical or life-critical functions where failure is not acceptable.

6. Compact size. Embedded systems must fit inside their host device. A microcontroller in a hearing aid is smaller than a fingernail. Size constraints mean embedded chips are integrated onto a single chip (System on a Chip, or SoC) rather than spread across a motherboard.

Key Fact

Embedded systems have six key characteristics: dedicated function (one specific task), real-time operation (guaranteed response time), low power consumption, low cost, high reliability and compact size. Contrast each with a general-purpose computer to nail compare questions.

Embedded Systems in Everyday Life

The following are examples of embedded systems you should be able to describe in detail:

Washing machine: The embedded system monitors the wash cycle, reads temperature and drum speed sensors, controls the motor speed, heater and water inlet valve, and advances through the programme stages in the correct order. The user selects a programme; the embedded system handles everything else automatically.

Traffic light controller: An embedded system manages traffic signal timing at a junction. It receives input from road sensors (detecting waiting vehicles), processes the current signal state, and outputs the correct sequence of red, amber and green signals to each set of lights — all in real time to keep traffic flowing safely.

Fitness band (activity tracker): Contains embedded sensors (accelerometer, heart rate monitor) and a microcontroller that reads these sensors, calculates steps, distance and heart rate, stores data and transmits it via Bluetooth to a smartphone. Runs on a small battery for days or weeks, so low power consumption is essential.

Microwave oven: The embedded system reads the keypad input, drives the display, controls the magnetron (the component that generates microwaves), runs the turntable motor and counts down the timer. When the timer reaches zero it stops the magnetron and sounds the beeper. No user programming is possible — the functions are fixed in firmware stored in ROM.

Engine Management Unit (EMU) in a car: One of the most sophisticated embedded systems in everyday use. It reads dozens of sensors (throttle position, oxygen level in exhaust, engine temperature, crankshaft speed) and makes real-time adjustments to fuel injection timing and quantity, ignition timing and emissions control. A typical modern car may contain over 100 separate embedded systems.

Key Fact

Every embedded system follows an input → process → output cycle. In a washing machine: sensors provide inputs (water temperature, drum speed), the processor makes decisions (increase heater power, change motor speed), and actuators carry out outputs (heater on/off, motor speed signal). This IPO structure appears in many exam questions.

Some embedded systems operate in environments where failure could cause serious harm. These are called safety-critical systems. Examples include:

  • Pacemakers — regulate the heartbeat of patients with heart conditions. A software bug or power failure could be fatal. Pacemakers are tested to an extremely high standard and their firmware is rarely if ever updated in the field.
  • Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) — prevent wheels from locking up during hard braking. The ABS microcontroller must respond within milliseconds or the system fails to prevent a skid.
  • Fly-by-wire flight control systems — modern passenger aircraft rely on embedded computers to translate pilot inputs into control surface movements. Multiple redundant systems run in parallel so that if one fails, another takes over immediately.

These safety-critical applications explain why embedded system software is subject to much more rigorous testing and formal verification than typical consumer software. The cost of failure is simply too high to tolerate bugs.

What Is a Computer Network?

A computer network is formed whenever two or more devices are connected so they can communicate. Networks are everywhere — your school uses one to share printers and the internet connection; hospitals use them to access patient records; banks rely on them to process transactions in real time. Understanding how networks are structured is a core part of GCSE Computer Science.

Characteristics of Networks

All networks share a common set of characteristics that define how they work and what they can do:

  • Shared resources — devices on a network can share hardware (printers, scanners), software (licences), and internet connections, reducing cost.
  • Communication — users can send messages and files directly to each other through email, messaging apps and shared drives.
  • Centralised storage — files saved to a network server can be accessed from any device on the network, making collaboration easier.
  • Security management — a network administrator can apply security policies, manage user accounts and monitor activity across all connected devices from one place.
Key Fact

The main advantages of networking are shared resources (hardware and internet), centralised data storage, easier communication between users, and the ability to apply security policies across all devices from one central point.

Network Topologies

A network topology describes the layout of a network — how devices are physically connected and how data travels between them. The four topologies you must know for your exam are star, mesh, ring and bus.

Star Topology

In a star topology, every device connects directly to a central switch or hub. Data from any device travels to the switch first, which then forwards it to the correct destination.

Advantages of star topology:

  • If one cable or device fails, the rest of the network keeps working — the fault is isolated.
  • Performance is consistent because each device has a dedicated link to the switch; one device’s traffic does not slow down another’s.
  • Adding new devices is straightforward — just plug another cable into the switch.

Disadvantages of star topology:

  • The central switch is a single point of failure — if it breaks, the entire network goes down.
  • More cabling is needed than in some other topologies, which increases cost.
  • The switch itself represents an additional hardware cost.

Star topology is the most common choice for modern wired networks in schools, offices and homes.

Mesh Topology

In a mesh topology, every device connects to multiple other devices, creating redundant paths for data. A full mesh connects every device to every other device; a partial mesh connects most devices but not all.

Advantages of mesh topology:

  • Highly reliable — if one path fails, data is automatically rerouted through another path.
  • There is no single point of failure, making mesh networks ideal for critical systems.
  • Data can travel across multiple routes simultaneously, increasing throughput.

Disadvantages of mesh topology:

  • Very expensive to install — a full mesh of ten devices requires 45 cables.
  • Complex to manage and configure, especially as the network grows.
Key Fact

Star topology relies on a central switch and is easy to manage but has a single point of failure at the switch. Mesh topology is highly reliable with no single point of failure but is expensive to cable and complex to manage.

In a ring topology, devices are connected in a closed loop. Data travels around the ring in one direction (or both directions in a dual ring), passing through each device until it reaches its destination.

Advantages of ring topology:

  • Data flows in an orderly manner — each device gets a turn to transmit, preventing collisions.
  • Performance is predictable and degrades gradually rather than suddenly as more devices are added.

Disadvantages of ring topology:

  • If one device or cable in the ring fails, the entire network is disrupted (unless a dual ring is used).
  • Adding or removing a device requires temporarily breaking the ring, causing downtime.
  • Data must travel through every intermediate device before reaching its destination, which can be slow on large networks.

Ring topology is rarely used in modern networks but remains a common exam topic.

In a bus topology, all devices connect to a single shared cable called the backbone. Data broadcast by any device travels along the entire cable and is read by all other devices, but only the intended recipient processes it. Terminators at each end of the cable absorb signals and prevent them from bouncing back.

Advantages of bus topology:

  • Simple and cheap to install — uses a single backbone cable.
  • Easy to extend by adding more devices to the backbone.

Disadvantages of bus topology:

  • If the backbone cable fails, the entire network stops working.
  • All devices share the same cable, so only one device can transmit at a time — heavy traffic causes collisions and slows the network significantly.
  • Performance degrades quickly as more devices are added.

Bus topology was common in early Ethernet networks but has been replaced by star topology in most modern installations.

Comparing the Four Topologies

When exam questions ask you to compare topologies, focus on three criteria: fault tolerance, cost and scalability.

TopologyFault toleranceCostScalability
StarHigh (switch fail only)MediumGood
MeshVery highHighPoor (cabling)
RingLow (one break halts all)Low–mediumPoor (needs downtime)
BusLow (backbone break halts all)LowPoor (collisions increase)

Why Network Hardware Matters

Every network is built from physical components that move data between devices. Understanding what each piece of hardware does — and why it differs from the others — is essential for your exam. You need to know six devices: router, hub, switch, bridge, wireless access point (WAP) and network interface card (NIC).

Routers

A router connects different networks together and directs data packets between them. When you type a web address at home, your router decides the best path for your request to take across the internet. Routers operate at the Network layer of the OSI model, reading IP addresses to make forwarding decisions.

Most home routers also include a switch, a wireless access point and a modem all in one device, but in larger business networks these functions are handled by separate pieces of hardware.

Switches

A switch connects multiple devices within a single network — for example, all the computers in one classroom. Unlike a hub, a switch is intelligent: it maintains a table of MAC addresses so it can send data directly to the correct device rather than broadcasting it to everyone. This makes switches far more efficient than hubs and is why they are standard in modern networks.

Hubs

A hub also connects multiple devices, but it has no intelligence. When a device sends data to the hub, the hub broadcasts it to every other connected device. The intended recipient reads it; all other devices discard it. This wastes bandwidth and creates security risks because any device can “hear” all traffic. Hubs have been almost entirely replaced by switches in real networks.

Key Fact

A switch uses a MAC address table to deliver data only to the correct destination device. A hub broadcasts data to every connected device. This is why switches are more efficient and more secure than hubs.

Bridges

A bridge connects two separate network segments and decides whether to forward or block data based on MAC addresses. If a frame is destined for a device on the same segment it came from, the bridge drops it; if it is destined for the other segment, the bridge forwards it. Bridges reduce unnecessary traffic crossing between segments and can connect different media types (for example, copper and fibre).

Bridges are similar to switches but operate between two segments rather than many ports. In modern networks, switches have largely replaced standalone bridges.

Wireless Access Points (WAPs)

A wireless access point (WAP) allows devices such as laptops, smartphones and tablets to join a wired network without a physical cable. The WAP translates between the wireless (Wi-Fi) and wired (Ethernet) protocols. In a large building such as a school, multiple WAPs are placed throughout to give full coverage, all connected back to the same wired network infrastructure.

Network Interface Cards (NICs)

A network interface card (NIC) is the hardware component inside every networked device — computer, printer, smart TV — that handles the connection to the network. Each NIC is assigned a globally unique MAC address at manufacture. This 48-bit address is used by switches and bridges to identify devices. Modern devices have both a wired NIC (Ethernet port) and a wireless NIC (Wi-Fi) built in.

Key Fact

The six network hardware components you must know are: router (connects networks, uses IP addresses), switch (connects devices in a network, uses MAC addresses), hub (broadcasts to all devices), bridge (joins two segments, filters by MAC), WAP (wireless to wired connection) and NIC (the hardware interface inside every device, with a unique MAC address).

Networks carry data over physical media (wired) or radio waves (wireless). Both have trade-offs that you may be asked to compare.

Wired (Ethernet) uses copper or fibre-optic cables to transmit data. Copper is cheaper but limited in speed and distance; fibre-optic uses pulses of light and offers much higher bandwidth over longer distances but is more expensive to install. Wired connections are more secure (a physical cable cannot easily be intercepted) and more reliable (no interference from walls or other devices).

Wireless (Wi-Fi) uses radio waves, allowing devices to connect without cables. This gives flexibility — users can move around while staying connected. However, wireless signals can be blocked by walls, interfered with by other devices using the same frequency, and intercepted more easily than a wired connection, creating security risks. Speed and range decrease with distance from the WAP.

A networking standard is an agreed set of rules that ensures devices from different manufacturers can communicate reliably. Without standards, a router from one company might not be able to talk to a switch from another.

The most important networking standards you need to know are:

  • IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) — defines how devices connect over wired cables and how they take turns to transmit data.
  • IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) — defines how wireless devices communicate using radio frequencies. The 802.11 family includes amendments for different speeds and frequencies (for example, 802.11ac operates on 5 GHz and supports speeds above 1 Gbps).

Standards are developed by international bodies such as the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) so that manufacturers worldwide follow the same rules. This means you can buy any Wi-Fi router and connect any Wi-Fi-certified device to it, regardless of manufacturer.

Why Layered Models Exist

Sending data across a network involves dozens of different tasks: converting a file to electrical signals, addressing packets, establishing connections, encrypting data, and presenting information on screen. The OSI model (Open Systems Interconnection model) organises these tasks into seven separate layers. Each layer has a clearly defined job and only needs to communicate with the layers directly above and below it. This makes networks easier to design, troubleshoot and develop: engineers can update one layer without rewriting the rest.

The 2024 examiners’ report highlighted OSI layer descriptions as a weak area — students could name layers but not describe what each one does. This lesson focusses on function, not just naming. A common mnemonic for the layers from bottom to top: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application).

Key Fact

The seven OSI layers from bottom to top are: Physical (1), Data Link (2), Network (3), Transport (4), Session (5), Presentation (6), Application (7). The mnemonic “Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away” helps you recall the correct order.

Layer 1 — Physical

The Physical layer is responsible for transmitting raw bits (0s and 1s) over a physical medium — copper cable, fibre-optic cable or radio waves. It defines the electrical signals, voltages, connector types and timing used to represent binary data. The Physical layer has no concept of structure or meaning; it simply transmits and receives signals.

Protocols and standards at this layer include Ethernet (cabling) and IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi radio). Hardware at this layer includes cables, repeaters and hubs.

Layer 2 — Data Link

The Data Link layer takes the raw bits from the Physical layer and organises them into frames. It handles node-to-node delivery within a single network segment, using MAC addresses to identify source and destination. The Data Link layer also performs basic error detection (not correction) to check whether a frame arrived without corruption.

Protocols at this layer include Ethernet (the framing standard for wired LANs) and Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11). Hardware: switches and bridges operate at this layer.

Layer 3 — Network

The Network layer is responsible for routing data across multiple networks from source to destination. It uses IP addresses (logical addresses) to identify devices globally and selects the best path for each packet. The data unit at this layer is a packet.

The key protocol at this layer is IP (Internet Protocol). Hardware: routers operate at this layer, reading IP addresses to decide where to forward each packet.

Layer 4 — Transport

The Transport layer manages end-to-end communication between applications on different hosts. It breaks data into segments and ensures they are reassembled correctly at the destination. It also handles flow control (preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver) and error recovery (requesting retransmission of lost segments).

Two key protocols operate here:

  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — connection-oriented. Before data is sent, TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake and guarantees delivery by acknowledging every segment. Used where accuracy matters: web pages (HTTP), email (SMTP), file transfer (FTP).
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol) — connectionless. Segments are sent without acknowledgement, so UDP is faster but unreliable. Used where speed matters more than accuracy: video streaming, online gaming, voice calls.
Key Fact

TCP (Transport layer) guarantees reliable, ordered delivery by acknowledging every segment — used by HTTP, SMTP and FTP. UDP sends segments without acknowledgement for speed — used by video streaming and online gaming. Both are Transport layer protocols.

Layer 5 — Session

The Session layer establishes, manages and terminates sessions (conversations) between applications. A session is an ongoing exchange: for example, a video call between two computers involves a session that keeps both sides synchronised. The Session layer also provides checkpointing — if a large data transfer fails midway, the transfer can resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch.

Layer 6 — Presentation

The Presentation layer is responsible for translating data between the format the application uses and the format the network requires. Its three main tasks are data translation (converting character encodings, for example between UTF-8 and ASCII), data compression (reducing size before transmission) and encryption (scrambling data for secure transmission). HTTPS encryption (TLS/SSL) is handled at this layer.

Layer 7 — Application

The Application layer is the topmost layer and the one users interact with directly. It provides the interface between the network and the software applications running on a device. This is where user-facing protocols operate.

Key Application layer protocols:

  • HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — transfers web pages between a server and a browser.
  • HTTPS (HTTP Secure) — HTTP with TLS encryption; used for secure web browsing and online transactions.
  • FTP (File Transfer Protocol) — transfers files between a client and a server.
  • SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — sends email from a client to a mail server or between mail servers.
  • POP3 / IMAP — retrieve email from a server. POP3 downloads and deletes from the server; IMAP keeps mail on the server and synchronises across devices.
  • DNS (Domain Name System) — translates human-readable domain names (e.g. studyvault.co.uk) into IP addresses.
  • DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — automatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network.

Use this table to review all seven layers before a practice exam:

LayerNameResponsibilityKey protocols / hardware

6PresentationTranslation, compression, encryptionTLS/SSL, JPEG, ASCII
5SessionStart, manage and end sessionsNetBIOS, checkpointing
4TransportEnd-to-end delivery, flow controlTCP, UDP
3NetworkRouting packets across networksIP — Routers
2Data LinkFrame delivery within a network segmentEthernet, Wi-Fi — Switches, Bridges
1PhysicalTransmit raw bits over a mediumCables, Hubs, Repeaters

Misconception 1: “HTTP is at the Transport layer.” HTTP is an Application layer protocol. The Transport layer is where TCP and UDP operate — HTTP runs on top of TCP at the Application layer.

Misconception 2: “Routers work at the Data Link layer.” Routers operate at the Network layer (layer 3), reading IP addresses. Switches operate at the Data Link layer (layer 2), reading MAC addresses.

Misconception 3: “Encryption happens at the Application layer.” Encryption is primarily a Presentation layer function (layer 6). TLS/SSL, used for HTTPS, is a Presentation layer service even though it is triggered by an Application layer protocol.

What Is Packet Switching?

When you send a large file or load a web page, the data is not sent as one continuous stream. Instead it is broken into small chunks called packets. Each packet travels independently through the network and may take a different route to the same destination. At the destination, the packets are reassembled in the correct order. This approach is called packet switching.

Packet switching was designed to be resilient: if one route through the network is congested or broken, packets are automatically sent via an alternative path. This makes it far more robust than circuit switching, which reserves a dedicated path for the entire duration of a call (as used in traditional telephone networks).

The Structure of a TCP/IP Packet

A packet has two main sections: the packet header and the packet payload.

The header contains:

  • Source IP address — the IP address of the sending device.
  • Destination IP address — the IP address of the receiving device.
  • Packet number / sequence number — used to reassemble packets in the correct order at the destination.
  • Time to Live (TTL) — a counter decremented by each router the packet passes through. When TTL reaches zero, the packet is discarded. This prevents packets looping forever if they get lost.
  • Error-checking data — a checksum value used by the destination to verify the packet arrived without corruption.

The payload carries the actual content — a portion of the file, image or web page being transmitted. Most packets carry between 500 and 1,500 bytes of payload data.

Key Fact

A packet header contains: source IP address, destination IP address, sequence number (for reassembly), Time to Live (TTL, prevents endless looping) and a checksum (error checking). The payload holds the actual data being sent.

How Packet Switching Works

When data is sent:

  1. The sending device breaks the data into packets and adds a header to each one.
  2. Each packet is sent into the network independently. Packets do not have to travel together.
  3. Each router the packet encounters reads the destination IP address in the header and forwards the packet towards its destination along the best available route.
  4. Packets from the same file may arrive at the destination in a different order from the one in which they were sent.
  5. The receiving device uses the sequence numbers in the headers to reassemble the packets in the correct order. If a packet is missing, TCP requests it to be resent.

The advantage of this approach is that the network can route packets around failures and congestion in real time. The internet would not function at global scale without packet switching.

Routing and Routing Cost Calculation

A routing cost is a value assigned to each link between two routers. When a packet needs to travel from source to destination, the router calculates the total cost of each possible path and chooses the path with the lowest total cost.

Routing cost can be based on different factors:

  • Hop count — the number of routers (hops) the packet must pass through. Fewer hops = lower cost.
  • Bandwidth — the capacity of the link. Higher bandwidth links are cheaper (faster).
  • Latency — the time taken for a packet to travel along the link. Lower latency = lower cost.
  • Congestion — a heavily used link has a higher cost.

Consider four routers: A, B, C and D. A packet needs to travel from A to D. The available links and their costs are:

LinkCost
A → B4
A → C2
B → D3
C → D6
C → B1

Possible paths from A to D:

  • Path 1: A → B → D — total cost = 4 + 3 = 7
  • Path 2: A → C → D — total cost = 2 + 6 = 8
  • Path 3: A → C → B → D — total cost = 2 + 1 + 3 = 6

The router would select Path 3 (A → C → B → D) with a total cost of 6 — the lowest. Note that this path goes through three hops, not two, but it is cheaper because the A→C and C→B links are low cost.

Exam tip: always write out all possible paths and add up their costs before identifying the lowest. Do not assume the path with fewest hops is always cheapest.

Routers use a routing table to look up the best path for each destination. There are two ways to populate this table:

Static routing — routes are manually configured by a network administrator. The path never changes unless an administrator updates it. Static routing is simple and predictable but cannot adapt to network failures automatically.

Dynamic routing — routers share information with each other using routing protocols and automatically update their tables when the network changes. If a link fails, dynamic routing finds an alternative path within seconds. Most large networks, including the internet, use dynamic routing.

Key Fact

To calculate the cheapest route in a network, list all possible paths from source to destination, add up the costs of all links on each path, and select the path with the lowest total. The cheapest path is not always the one with the fewest hops.

lesson_title: The Internet: DNS, URLs and the Web Browser
content_html:
The Internet and the World Wide Web

The internet is the global infrastructure of connected networks. The World Wide Web (web) is a service that runs on top of the internet — a collection of web pages stored on servers and accessed via browsers using HTTP or HTTPS. The internet also carries email, file transfers, video calls and many other services. The web is just one part of the internet, not the whole thing.

IP Addresses and the Problem They Create

Every device connected to the internet has an IP address — a unique numerical label such as 142.250.187.78. IP addresses allow routers to deliver data to the correct destination. However, humans cannot easily memorise long strings of numbers, which is why the Domain Name System exists.

The Domain Name System (DNS)

The Domain Name System (DNS) works like a phone book for the internet. When you type a web address, your device does not know the IP address of that server — it asks a DNS server to look it up. DNS is distributed across millions of servers worldwide so that no single server needs to know every domain name.

The DNS resolution process works in this sequence:

  1. Browser cache check — the browser first checks its own cache. If you visited the site recently, the IP address is already stored locally.
  2. Resolver (ISP’s DNS server) — if not cached, the request goes to a DNS resolver, typically provided by your ISP. The resolver also has its own cache.
  3. Root name server — if the resolver does not know the address, it contacts a root name server. The root server does not know the final IP address, but it knows which server handles the top-level domain (e.g. .co.uk or .com).
  4. TLD (top-level domain) server — the root server directs the resolver to the relevant TLD server, which handles all domains ending in .co.uk, .com and so on.
  5. Authoritative name server — the TLD server directs the resolver to the authoritative name server for the specific domain. This server holds the actual IP address record and returns it to the resolver.
  6. Response — the resolver returns the IP address to your browser, which then makes a direct request to the web server at that IP address. The result is cached for future use.
Key Fact

DNS resolution order: browser cache → resolver (ISP) → root name server → TLD server → authoritative name server → IP address returned to browser. Caching at each stage speeds up future requests for the same domain.

URL Structure

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the full address used to locate a resource on the web. Each part of a URL has a specific meaning:

Consider the example URL: https://www.studyvault.co.uk/lesson/computer-science/networks

  • Protocol: https:// — tells the browser which communication protocol to use. HTTPS indicates an encrypted, secure connection (HTTP without the S is unencrypted).
  • Subdomain: www — the host within the domain, conventionally www for web servers.
  • Domain name: studyvault.co.uk — identifies the organisation. The TLD (.co.uk) indicates a commercial UK site.
  • Path: /lesson/computer-science/networks — the location of the specific resource on the server, like a folder path on a hard drive.
Key Fact

A URL has four main parts: protocol (https://), subdomain (www), domain name (e.g. bbc.co.uk) and path (/news/technology). The protocol tells the browser how to communicate; the domain name identifies the server; the path specifies the exact resource.

What a Web Browser Does

A web browser is the software that fetches and displays web pages. When you enter a URL:

  1. The browser resolves the domain name to an IP address using DNS.
  2. The browser sends an HTTP GET request to the web server at that IP address, asking for the web page.
  3. The server responds with the HTML, CSS and JavaScript files that make up the page.
  4. The browser’s rendering engine interprets the HTML structure, applies the CSS styling and executes the JavaScript to produce the page you see on screen.

Browsers also manage cookies (small files that store session data and preferences), maintain a browsing history and cache previously visited pages to speed up future loads.

HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) transfers web page data between a client and server. It transmits data in plain text, meaning any attacker who intercepts the packets can read the content.

HTTPS (HTTP Secure) uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) to encrypt the connection. The server presents a digital certificate that proves its identity; the browser and server then negotiate an encryption key. All subsequent data is encrypted, so even if a packet is intercepted, the attacker sees only scrambled data. HTTPS is mandatory for any site handling passwords, payment details or personal information.

Browsers display a padlock icon in the address bar when HTTPS is in use. The presence of HTTPS alone does not guarantee a site is legitimate — a phishing site can use HTTPS too. However, a site without HTTPS is definitely not secure for sending sensitive data.

Misconception: “The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.” The internet is the network infrastructure; the web is one service that runs on it. Email, FTP and online gaming also use the internet but are not part of the web.

Misconception: “DNS converts a URL into an IP address.” DNS converts a domain name (e.g. bbc.co.uk) into an IP address. The full URL includes the protocol and path, which are not part of the DNS lookup — only the domain portion is sent to the DNS server.

Misconception: “HTTPS means a website is safe to use.” HTTPS encrypts the connection but says nothing about the trustworthiness of the site itself. A fraudulent site can and does use HTTPS.

Why Cybersecurity Matters

Every connected device is a potential target. Attackers have financial, political or personal motivations to steal data, disrupt services or hold organisations to ransom. Understanding how attacks work is the first step towards defending against them. Your exam expects you to describe specific threats, explain how each works, and match it with appropriate defences.

Malware

Malware (malicious software) is a broad term covering any software designed to harm a system or its users. Key types include:

  • Virus — attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is shared. It requires a host file and user action to propagate.
  • Worm — spreads automatically across a network without needing a host file or user action, exploiting security vulnerabilities.
  • Trojan — disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it. Once active, it can open a backdoor for an attacker.
  • Ransomware — encrypts a victim’s files and demands payment (a ransom) for the decryption key.
  • Spyware — secretly monitors user activity, capturing keystrokes, passwords and browsing habits, and sends this data to an attacker.

Phishing and Social Engineering

Phishing attacks impersonate trusted organisations — banks, delivery companies, employers — using convincing but fraudulent emails or websites. The goal is to steal login credentials, financial details or personal information.

Social engineering is the broader category that phishing belongs to. Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Variants include:

  • Spear phishing — a targeted phishing attack aimed at a specific individual, using personal information to appear more convincing.
  • Pretexting — the attacker invents a scenario (e.g. pretending to be IT support) to gain the victim’s trust and extract information.
  • Baiting — leaving infected storage devices (e.g. USB sticks) in public places, hoping a curious person will plug one in.
Key Fact

Phishing uses deceptive emails or websites that impersonate trusted organisations to trick users into submitting passwords or financial details. It is a form of social engineering — it exploits human trust rather than technical flaws.

Brute-Force Attacks

A brute-force attack systematically tries every possible password or key until the correct one is found. Modern computers can try billions of combinations per second, making short or simple passwords easy to crack. Dictionary attacks are a faster variant that uses common words and passwords first rather than every character combination.

Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed DoS (DDoS)

A Denial of Service (DoS) attack overwhelms a server with requests until it can no longer respond to genuine users. A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack uses a botnet — thousands of infected devices controlled by the attacker — to send traffic simultaneously, making it far harder to block because the traffic comes from many sources.

DoS/DDoS attacks target availability: the victim’s website or service becomes inaccessible. Financial services, gaming platforms and news sites are common targets.

Data Interception

Data interception (sometimes called a man-in-the-middle attack) occurs when an attacker secretly captures data travelling between two parties. On unsecured Wi-Fi networks, an attacker can intercept packets and read unencrypted data such as login credentials sent over HTTP. Using a rogue access point — a fake Wi-Fi hotspot — is one method attackers use to position themselves between a victim and the internet.

SQL Injection

SQL injection targets web applications that use databases. Many websites use SQL (Structured Query Language) to retrieve data — for example, when a user logs in, the application queries the database for matching credentials. If the input is not properly validated, an attacker can insert SQL commands into a form field to bypass authentication, extract data or delete records.

For example, entering ' OR '1'='1 as a username can trick a poorly written login query into returning all user records, granting access without a valid password.

Key Fact

The seven main threats you must know are: malware (malicious software), phishing/social engineering (psychological deception), brute-force attacks (exhaustive password guessing), DoS/DDoS (flooding a server), data interception (capturing network traffic), and SQL injection (manipulating database queries via input fields).

Defences fall into two categories: technical (software and hardware controls) and procedural (policies and user behaviour).

Anti-malware software scans files and network traffic for known malware signatures and suspicious behaviour. It must be kept up to date because new malware variants are released constantly.

Firewalls monitor incoming and outgoing network traffic and block packets that do not meet defined security rules. A firewall can block traffic from suspicious IP addresses and prevent unauthorised access to internal systems. Firewalls are the first line of defence against DoS attacks and many forms of intrusion.

User access levels limit what each user account can see and do. Principle of least privilege — granting users only the permissions they need for their role — reduces the damage if an account is compromised.

Strong passwords and two-factor authentication (2FA) defend against brute-force attacks. Long, complex passwords take vastly longer to crack; 2FA requires a second verification step (such as a code sent to a mobile device) even if the password is stolen.

Encryption protects data in transit (e.g. HTTPS/TLS) and at rest (e.g. encrypting stored files). Even if data is intercepted or a device is stolen, encrypted data cannot be read without the decryption key.

Penetration testing involves authorised security professionals deliberately attempting to break into a system to identify vulnerabilities before a real attacker does. The findings are used to patch weaknesses before they can be exploited.

Network forensics is the process of capturing and analysing network traffic logs after a security incident to determine how an attack occurred, what data was accessed and who was responsible. It supports incident response and legal proceedings.

Exam questions often ask you to match a defence to a specific threat. Use this table as a revision reference:

ThreatKey defence(s)
MalwareAnti-malware software, user access levels, email filtering
Phishing / social engineeringUser education and training, email filters, 2FA
Brute-forceStrong passwords, account lockout policies, 2FA
DoS / DDoSFirewall (traffic filtering), rate limiting, cloud-based mitigation
Data interceptionEncryption (HTTPS/TLS), VPN, avoid unsecured Wi-Fi
SQL injectionInput validation / sanitisation, parameterised queries, penetration testing

Why Does Data Need a Type?

Every piece of data stored in a computer has a data type. The type tells the computer how many bytes to reserve, which operations are allowed, and how the binary pattern in memory should be interpreted. A sequence of bits can mean a whole number, a fraction, a letter or a logical true/false value — the data type is what determines the meaning.

The Five Core Data Types

Your exam requires you to know five data types:

  • Integer — a whole number, positive or negative, with no decimal point. Examples: 42, −7, 0. Stored in a fixed number of bytes (often 2 or 4).
  • Real (also called float) — a number that can have a fractional part. Examples: 3.14, −0.5, 100.0. Stored using a floating-point representation that can handle a vast range of values.
  • Character — a single symbol: a letter, digit, space or punctuation mark. Stored as a numeric code (see the lesson on ASCII and Unicode). Example: ‘A’ is stored as the number 65.
  • String — a sequence of zero or more characters. Examples: “hello”, “42”, “” (empty string). Strings are stored as consecutive character codes in memory.
  • Boolean — a value that can only be True or False. Used in conditions and logic. Stored as a single bit (1 for True, 0 for False), though in practice a full byte is often reserved.
Key Fact

The five data types you must know are: integer (whole number), real (decimal number), character (single symbol), string (sequence of characters) and Boolean (True or False). Choosing the wrong type wastes memory or causes errors.

Number Systems: Denary, Binary and Hexadecimal

Computers process everything in binary (base 2), but humans normally count in denary (base 10, using digits 0–9). A third system, hexadecimal (base 16, using 0–9 then A–F), gives programmers a compact way to read and write binary patterns. One hex digit always represents exactly four binary bits (a nibble).

Hex digit to denary and binary equivalents
